domains.name: Monetization: Pricing AI Right

scenarios.title: The Margin Surprise
scenarios.situation: Your AI support product charges $49/seat/month. Your biggest customer has 20 seats but their power users generate 40,000 queries a month. Your infrastructure bill just exceeded their contract value.
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural pricing mistake?
choices: Per-seat pricing decoupled from inference cost: heavy usage by a few seats destroys margin. Fix with hybrid pricing — seat base plus usage tiers or query allowances per seat, so cost and price scale together.
The customer is abusing the product; throttle them.
Raise seat prices for everyone.
Switch to a cheaper model and hope quality holds.
scenarios.why: The correct approach ties price to the cost driver: when marginal cost is per query, price must have a per-query component. Hybrid packaging (base + usage) keeps the deal predictable for the buyer while protecting margin against power-law usage.
scenarios.hint: What actually drives your cost — seats or queries?
evidence: 20 seats x $49 = $980/mo revenue; 40k queries x $0.03 = $1,200/mo cost

scenarios.title: The 80% Cost Cut
scenarios.situation: Analysis shows 60% of your AI queries are near-duplicates: same questions, same documents, slightly different wording. Inference is your largest COGS line.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage cost move?
choices: Remove the feature that generates the queries.
Semantic caching: cache responses keyed on meaning, not exact text — serve paraphrased repeats from cache at ~1% of inference cost. Pair with prompt compression and model routing for the remainder.
Negotiate a bigger discount with the model provider.
Raise prices to cover the cost.
scenarios.why: The correct approach attacks the cost structure, not the price: semantic caching converts the repeat-query majority into near-zero marginal cost. Provider discounts help at the margin; caching changes the shape of the curve.
scenarios.hint: What fraction of your inference spend is literally answering the same question twice?

scenarios.title: The Outcome Pricing Trap
scenarios.situation: You price your AI recruiting product per hire made. Customers love it. But 'hire made' is disputed constantly: they claim the AI only sourced, they closed — and your revenue swings wildly quarter to quarter.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this outcome model?
choices: Customers are dishonest; add legal enforcement.
Lower the per-hire price to reduce disputes.

The outcome lacks a trusted, attributable measurement: pricing on a disputed, lagging, multi-causal outcome creates endless conflict and revenue volatility. Price on a leading, attributable proxy (qualified interviews scheduled) or hybridize with a platform fee.
Outcome pricing never works; go back to seats.
scenarios.why: The correct approach keeps outcome pricing only where the outcome is measurable and attributable by both sides. A leading indicator the product directly produces (interviews scheduled, tickets resolved) preserves value-alignment without the attribution war; a platform fee stabilizes the base.
scenarios.hint: Can both sides independently verify the billing event?

scenarios.title: The Generous Free Tier
scenarios.situation: Your free tier allows 10,000 AI queries a month. Conversion to paid is 0.3%. Power users happily run production workloads on free accounts.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Remove the free tier entirely.
Add more features to the free tier to attract users.
Advertise the paid tier more aggressively.

Cap free on the value metric at the 'real usage starts here' line: cut to ~500 queries, add the watermark/team features as paid-only, and trigger upgrade nudges at quota moments. Free is for evaluation, not production.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the free tier as a funnel, not a product: the cap should sit just past the magic moment, so growing success pushes users into paid. A 10k-query free tier is an unlimited tier with extra steps.
scenarios.hint: At what usage level has a free user proven they get value?
objectives: Place upgrade triggers at value moments
evidence: 0.3% free-to-paid; top free accounts use 9,800 queries/mo

scenarios.title: The Enterprise Ask
scenarios.situation: A Fortune 500 prospect wants your AI product but demands: SSO/SAML, audit logs, data residency in the EU, a 99.9% SLA, and a security review — for a 50-seat pilot.
scenarios.prompt: How do you package and price this?
choices: Enterprise tier: bundle SSO, audit, residency, and SLA as the enterprise package at 3-5x the Pro seat price with an annual commit — the compliance features ARE the product for this segment, and the security review cost is amortized across the contract.
Give them everything on the Pro plan to win the logo.
Refuse; enterprise is too much work for 50 seats.
Build each request as a custom one-off.
scenarios.why: The correct approach productizes enterprise requirements instead of customizing them: a versioned enterprise tier turns compliance cost into a priced package, the annual commit funds the security review, and the logo becomes a repeatable segment — not a one-off science project.
scenarios.hint: Which of these requests will the NEXT enterprise buyer also make?
objectives: Use annual commits to fund diligence
evidence: 50 seats; security review estimated at 60 engineering hours

scenarios.title: The Silent Cost Spike
scenarios.situation: After a 'small' prompt improvement, your inference bill jumps 60% with no usage growth. The new prompt adds few-shot examples and asks for detailed reasoning on every query.
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what is the discipline?
choices: Roll back the improvement; quality is not worth it.

Token bloat: few-shot examples and verbose reasoning multiply input AND output tokens per query. Discipline: measure cost-per-query in CI for every prompt change, set token budgets per feature, and route simple queries to smaller models.
The provider raised prices secretly.
Usage actually grew; the dashboard is wrong.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats prompts as cost-bearing code: every token has a price, and prompt changes need the same cost review as infrastructure changes. Token budgets and per-query cost metrics in CI catch bloat before it ships; model routing keeps simple queries cheap.
scenarios.hint: How many tokens did the 'small' change add per query?

scenarios.title: The Seat Expansion Stall
scenarios.situation: Your per-seat AI product is deployed at a 500-person company but only 60 people use it — the AI does the work, so teams need FEWER seats. Revenue per account is shrinking as the product succeeds.
scenarios.prompt: What pricing evolution fixes the misalignment?
choices: Raise per-seat prices to compensate.
Accept the shrink; it is the nature of automation.

Shift the value metric from seats to outcomes or usage: platform fee plus per-automation or per-resolution pricing — so customer success (fewer humans needed) grows your revenue instead of shrinking it.
Force minimum seat counts in contracts.
scenarios.why: The correct approach aligns price with the value you create: when AI reduces headcount, seat pricing punishes your own success. Usage or outcome pricing turns efficiency gains into expansion revenue — the customer saves money AND you grow.
scenarios.hint: Does your revenue grow or shrink when the customer needs fewer people?
evidence: 500 employees, 60 seats, declining; AI handles 70% of the workflow

scenarios.title: The Monthly Churn Drip
scenarios.situation: Your AI product is monthly-billed, $99/seat. Churn is 6% monthly — customers love the product but re-evaluate every invoice, and usage-based bills cause monthly sticker shock.
scenarios.prompt: What packaging change improves retention and predictability?
choices: Lower the monthly price.
Hide the usage breakdown from invoices.
Lock customers in with annual contracts and no discount.

Annual plans with commit tiers: 2 months free for annual prepay, usage included up to a generous allowance with predictable overage — the commit smooths revenue, the allowance kills bill shock, and annual buyers churn far less.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses packaging to change the buying psychology: annual commits convert twelve churn decisions into one, included allowances make bills predictable, and the discount is funded by the retention gain. Lowering price without changing structure keeps the churn machine running.
scenarios.hint: How many churn decisions does each billing model force per year?
evidence: 6% monthly churn; top reason: 're-evaluating spend' after variable invoices

lessons.title: LLM APIs — Core concepts
concepts: Roles are the API's instruction hierarchy: system sets the frame, user fills it.

System prompts: the system message carries the durable contract — persona, behavioral rules, output format — applied to every turn; user messages carry the per-request task. Manage it: keep the system prompt (it's the contract), keep recent turns verbatim, summarize or truncate the middle (sliding window + rolling summary).

Temperature rescales the token probability distribution before sampling: near 0 collapses toward the most likely token (deterministic, factual tasks), higher values spread probability (creative variation).

Structured output: tool calling is a loop, not magic: you declare tools as JSON schemas; the model emits structured tool_call intents; YOUR code executes the function and returns the result as a tool message; the model continues with the new facts.
JSON mode / structured-output parameters constrain decoding to a schema — the API guarantees shape-valid JSON, not just likely JSON.

example.code:
# invoice parser: same invoice gives different totals on reruns
response = client.chat(messages=messages, temperature=1.0)
example.walkthrough: Temperature rescales the token probability distribution before sampling: near 0 collapses toward the most likely token (deterministic, factual tasks), higher values spread probability (creative variation). A parser at temperature=1.0 samples freely — hence drifting totals. For extraction/classification, use temperature ~0 (plus a fixed seed where supported); reserve higher temperatures for brainstorming.

pitfalls: Common trap: request structured output (JSON mode / response schema) and validate against a schema.
Common trap: manage the context window deliberately: summarize or truncate older turns, keep the system prompt and recent turns, use sliding windows.
Common trap: API keys can't be stolen from client code.
Common trap: embed the API key in the frontend bundle.

lessons.title: Prompt Engineering — Core concepts
concepts: Few-shot examples demonstrate the exact input→output mapping — including edge cases (European decimals, missing fields) that instructions describe ambiguously. For logic/math/planning tasks, 'think step by step' (or few-shot reasoning traces) is the highest-leverage prompt change.
Chain-of-thought allocates intermediate tokens as working memory: each step becomes context for the next, so errors compound less and the model can 'check' its path.
Reasoning: (For production, pair with verification — reasoning can also rationalize wrong answers.).
Iteration: version the prompts, keep the eval set frozen during iteration, and beware overfitting to the eval set itself — hold out fresh examples for final validation.
Prompt evals: explicit constraints (length, audience, format template, forbidden content) make output gradable and consistent — the prompt becomes a specification, not a wish.

example.code:
# step 1: extract fields (JSON mode)
# step 2: validate totals (deterministic code)
# step 3: summarize for the dashboard
example.walkthrough: Decompose when stages have different natures: extraction (LLM + JSON mode) → validation (deterministic code, not the model!) → summarization (LLM). Each stage is testable, the deterministic parts are exact, and failures localize. A mega-prompt entangles everything — one weak stage poisons the whole output opaquely.

pitfalls: Common trap: one giant prompt for the whole task.
Common trap: write one perfect prompt on the first try.
Common trap: zero-shot with a longer system prompt.
Common trap: put the untrusted content first.

lessons.title: RAG Basics — Core concepts
concepts: Chunking splits documents into retrievable units (a few hundred tokens with overlap to preserve boundaries); each chunk is embedded, and the query retrieves the top-k by cosine similarity.

Embeddings: whole-document embeddings dilute the signal — the warranty paragraph's meaning drowns in 200 pages. Dense embeddings capture meaning but blur exact tokens — XR-2000, XR-1000, and XR-3000 are semantically adjacent.

Retrieval: top-k retrieval (k=5-10 typical) with re-ranking balances recall against context dilution: too few misses multi-part answers, too many buries the signal in noise and cost. Hybrid retrieval runs both and fuses rankings (e.g., reciprocal rank fusion): semantics for 'warranty terms', keywords for 'XR-2000'.
RAG motivation: production RAG is hybrid by default; pure dense is the demo version. A RAG system is only as fresh as its index pipeline — stale vectors are stale answers.

# TODO: retrieval design

Sentence-chunks are too small to be self-contained. Chunk size is the core RAG tuning knob: big enough for context, small enough for precision.

pitfalls: Common trap: check groundedness: verify each claim in the answer against the retrieved chunks (citation coverage, NLI entailment, or LLM-judge with the sources).
Common trap: RAG grounds the answer in retrieved documents: retrieve the relevant chunks, generate with them as context, cite sources.
Common trap: retrieve top-k (e.g., 5-10), optionally re-rank, and stuff the winners into the prompt with citations.
Common trap: embed the whole document as one vector.

lessons.title: Agent Loops — Core concepts
concepts: Agent loops need explicit bounds: max iterations (a circuit breaker on runaway reasoning), per-step timeouts (a hung tool shouldn't hang the agent), and progress detection (same action three times = stuck).
Least privilege applies to agents: each tool is both attack surface (prompt-injected instructions reaching delete_db) and confusion surface (40 similar tools → wrong-tool calls).
Tool design: stop conditions are part of the design, not pessimism. Design tools like API endpoints: minimal, well-described, permissioned.
Human-in-the-loop gates belong at irreversibility: sending, deleting, purchasing, publishing — actions with external consequences get approval; reads, drafts, and analysis run autonomously.

example.code:
# plan: [search docs, read file, edit file]
# observation: file doesn't exist -> agent edits a different file anyway
example.walkthrough: The ReAct loop is plan → act → observe → re-plan: each observation updates the plan. Blindly executing a stale plan (editing the wrong file because step 2 assumed step 1's result) is the signature agent failure mode. The plan is a working hypothesis, not a contract.

pitfalls: Common trap: detect the stuck pattern (same action, same error) and escalate: try a different approach N times, then stop and report.
Common trap: give the minimal tool set for the task, with narrowly-scoped permissions.
Common trap: the agent should act on everything autonomously.
Common trap: require human confirmation for irreversible/high-stakes actions (send, delete, purchase, publish).

lessons.title: Evals — Core concepts
concepts: Golden datasets: a golden dataset — curated inputs with expected outputs, covering typical cases, edge cases, and known failures — turns 'seems good' into a score.

LLM-as-judge works when treated as a measurement instrument: a detailed rubric (what earns each score), the reference sources for groundedness checks, and human spot-checks measuring judge-human agreement.

Eval CI: model selection is a three-way tradeoff: quality (eval score), cost per request (at your volume, 10x is real money), and latency (3.2s changes the UX). 'Eval once at launch' misses drift; 'eval on complaint' is incident-driven development.

Regression: evals in CI on every prompt/model change make AI behavior regression-tested like code: the PR shows the score delta before merge. Re-run it on every prompt/model change: improvements and regressions become visible numbers.

Without it, every iteration is a guess and regressions ship silently. The dataset is the test suite for non-deterministic software.

pitfalls: Common trap: the model vendor handles all safety.
Common trap: measure retrieval (recall@k, precision) and generation (faithfulness, correctness) separately.

lessons.title: AI Coding Workflows — Core concepts
concepts: Context is the agent's working memory: include the files being changed, their direct dependencies (interfaces, types, callers), and a crisp spec of the desired behavior.

Code review: require tests alongside the implementation (TDD-style: spec → tests → code works well with agents), review the tests' assertions (do they check the right behavior?), and keep them green in CI.
Principle: the whole repo drowns the signal in noise (and cost); a lone file starves it of contracts.
Apply the workflow deliberately: choose the right level of AI assistance for each task — full generation for boilerplate, pair-programming for logic, review-only for critical paths.

example.code:
# Goal: retry failed payments
# Acceptance: 3 retries, exponential backoff, idempotency key preserved
# Constraints: no new dependencies
example.walkthrough: A written spec — goal, acceptance criteria, constraints — converts 'add retries' from a wish into a verifiable target: the agent's output is checkable against the criteria, and surprises shrink. Vague prompts delegate every design decision to sampling. This is spec-driven development: the human decides what good looks like; the agent does the typing.

pitfalls: Common trap: the human owns architecture (boundaries, patterns, tradeoffs); the agent implements within them.
Common trap: keep agent diffs small and review every line.
Common trap: the agent needs real credentials to test.
Common trap: never paste secrets, keys, or credentials into the model.

lessons.title: AI Product Management — Core concepts
concepts: LLMs are fluent, not factual: they generate plausible text, so every factual claim in your product needs grounding — retrieval, citations, or verification — not a stricter prompt.
Evals are the product spec: a golden set sampled from real user queries, task-appropriate metrics, and regression runs on every prompt or model change — no evals, no ship.
RAG for fresh knowledge, fine-tuning for stable behavior: retrieve when documents change weekly; fine-tune when you need consistent tone, format, or domain behavior the base model lacks.
Design the UX around uncertainty: show sources, frame confidence honestly, make corrections easy, and route high-stakes actions to humans.
Responsible AI is a feature list: PII redaction before storage, bias spot-checks on real queries, usage policies, audit logs, and a clear escalation path when the model is out of its depth.

example.walkthrough: A tiny golden set of question/expected-answer pairs, a simple contains-check judge, and one aggregate score. Run it on every prompt change — a drop here catches regressions before your users do.

pitfalls: Common trap: shipping on vibes — 'it looked good in the playground' is not an eval.
Common trap: trusting retrieved documents blindly — third-party content can carry injected instructions.
Common trap: logging full prompts with PII and keeping them forever.
Common trap: letting a confident tone substitute for citations — users can't verify what they can't see.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Ai Product move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
