lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it top to bottom: each domain builds on the previous one, and later scenarios assume earlier knowledge
Every lesson ends with a knowledge check: answer correctly and the lesson auto-completes. Wrong answers send you back to review — this is verification, not clicking through
Scenarios are timed decision exercises with evidence to examine. Treat each like the real thing: read everything, decide, then commit
Your progress saves automatically. Domains unlock as you complete prerequisites — the path guides you, but you set the pace

example.code:
LEARN path: lessons -> scenarios -> labs -> drills
TERMINAL: hands-on command practice
MOCK: full timed assessment when ready

Suggested daily loop:
  1. Complete 2-3 lessons (with knowledge checks)
  2. Work 3-5 scenarios in those domains
  3. Run 1 lab end-to-end
  4. 10 minutes of drills
example.walkthrough: The bootcamp mirrors how professionals actually work: learn the concept, apply it under realistic conditions, then prove it in the lab. Skipping straight to the mock without the lessons is the fastest way to fail it.

pitfalls: Skipping lessons and jumping to scenarios — the scenarios assume lesson knowledge
Treating the knowledge check as a formality instead of a real self-test
Ignoring the terminal and labs — hands-on reps are where durable skill comes from
lessons.try_it: Open the Learn path and complete the first lesson's knowledge check to see auto-completion in action.

lessons.title: assessment Strategy: How to Win
concepts: The assessment rewards applied understanding over memorization — every domain here maps to something you will actually be asked to do
Time management wins: in timed assessments, bank the easy wins first, flag the hard ones, and never leave a question blank
Wrong answers are data: each missed scenario reveals a specific gap. Log it, revisit the lesson, and re-attempt until the pattern clicks
Sleep and spacing beat cramming: 90-minute focused sessions with breaks outperform marathon sessions, especially the week before assessment day

example.code:
The 3-pass method for timed assessments:
  Pass 1 (40% of time): answer everything you know cold
  Pass 2 (40% of time): work the flagged mediums with evidence
  Pass 3 (20% of time): educated guesses on the rest

Never spend 10 minutes on one question while five easy ones wait.
example.walkthrough: Elimination is a skill: practice ruling out two wrong choices fast, then deciding between the final two. Most scenario questions are designed so two options are clearly wrong to a prepared candidate.

pitfalls: Changing answers without new evidence — your first instinct after study is usually right
Perfectionism on one hard question while easy points expire
Studying new material the night before instead of reviewing what you know
lessons.try_it: Do one full timed mock this week using the 3-pass method, even before you feel ready. Baseline yourself.

lessons.title: Course Map: What You Will Master
concepts: This bootcamp has 15+ domains covering the full AI Product landscape — from foundations to the capstone project
Core domains teach the must-know systems; the Systems Anatomy domain teaches you to see them as living, connected flows
The capstone project proves you can build and operate a real system end-to-end — this is your interview story
The mock assessment simulates the real assessment so there are no surprises on the day

example.code:
AI Product mastery map:
  Foundations -> Core systems (domains 2-10)
  -> Systems Anatomy (see it all connected)
  -> Capstone (build it yourself)
  -> Mock (prove it under pressure)
example.walkthrough: Start with: LLM APIs. It unlocks everything downstream — the path is sequential for a reason.

pitfalls: Treating all domains as equal — weight your time toward the heaviest-tested areas
Skipping Systems Anatomy — it is the differentiator between passing and excelling
Saving the capstone for 'later' — start it early, iterate as you learn
lessons.try_it: Skim the domain list in the Learn path and note which three domains matter most for your goal. Start there after Start Here.

lessons.title: Problem Framing: AI Is Not the Product
concepts: Start from the job-to-be-done, not the model: 'reduce support handle time' is a product; 'an LLM chatbot' is a technology looking for a problem
The AI value test: does intelligence change the outcome 10x versus rules or search? If a regex solves it, ship the regex — AI is expensive, slow, and non-deterministic
Map the workflow before the model: where does a human currently decide, and is that decision frequent, painful, and data-rich enough to automate?
Write the press release first (working backwards): the future headline forces you to name the customer, the pain, and the measurable win

example.code:
Framing canvas:
  CUSTOMER: support leads at 200-seat SaaS companies
  JOB: resolve repetitive tickets without hiring
  TODAY: macros + copy-paste, 12 min/ticket
  AI WIN: draft answers from knowledge base, 4 min/ticket
  10x TEST: yes — language understanding is the bottleneck
example.walkthrough: The most common AI product failure is a solution in search of a problem: a demo that wows and a product nobody buys. If you cannot name the workflow, the pain's dollar cost, and why rules fail, you do not have a product yet — you have a demo.

pitfalls: Leading with model capabilities instead of customer pain
Automating a workflow nobody does frequently enough to matter
Skipping the 10x test — marginal gains do not justify AI's cost and risk
lessons.try_it: Take one AI feature idea and run the framing canvas: customer, job, today-state, AI win, 10x test.

lessons.title: Defensibility: Your Moat in the AI Era
concepts: Models are commoditizing: today's frontier advantage is next year's API price cut — moats must live elsewhere
Data moats: proprietary feedback loops (every user correction improves YOUR model), exclusive data access, and workflow-embedded context competitors cannot scrape
Distribution moats: embedded in the workflow (the copilot inside the tool they already open), network effects, and switching costs from integrations
Execution moats: evals, domain-tuned reliability, and operational excellence — 'it actually works in production' is a moat most AI startups lack

example.code:
Moat audit:
  Model: parity in 12 months (not a moat)
  Data: 2M labeled support resolutions (moat)
  Distribution: embedded in helpdesk (moat)
  Reliability: 99.2% grounded answers (moat)

Invest where the moat compounds.
example.walkthrough: Ask the uncomfortable question: if a frontier lab shipped your exact feature tomorrow, what would keep your customers? If the honest answer is 'nothing,' your roadmap's first job is building the answer — usually data, distribution, or reliability depth.

pitfalls: Believing the model choice is the moat
Collecting data with no plan to convert it into a feedback loop
Ignoring distribution — best model loses to best-distributed product
lessons.try_it: Run the moat audit on an AI product you know: what survives a frontier lab shipping the same feature?

lessons.title: Build vs Buy vs Wrap
concepts: Buy (API): fastest to market, zero infra burden — right when the model is not your differentiator and latency/cost fit
Build (fine-tune/self-host): justified when you need data privacy, cost at scale, latency control, or behavior the APIs cannot produce
Wrap honestly: a thin UX over an API is a valid product IF the value is in workflow, distribution, or data — invalid if the pitch is 'better AI'
The hybrid default: buy the foundation model, build the retrieval, evals, UX, and feedback loops — that is where most AI product value actually lives

example.code:
Decision matrix:
  Differentiator = model behavior? -> consider fine-tune
  Differentiator = workflow/data? -> buy model, build the rest
  Volume > 10M queries/mo? -> price self-host vs API
  Regulated data? -> self-host or VPC deployment

Default: buy foundation, build product.
example.walkthrough: Revisit the decision every 6 months: API prices fall, open models improve, and your volume changes the math. The build-vs-buy answer has an expiry date — calendar the review.

pitfalls: Fine-tuning before proving the product works with prompting + RAG
Self-hosting for 'control' at 10k queries a month — negative ROI
Never revisiting the decision as prices and volumes move
lessons.try_it: Score one AI feature on the decision matrix: buy, build, or hybrid? Write the one-paragraph justification.

lessons.title: Roadmapping Under Model Uncertainty
concepts: Model capabilities shift quarterly: roadmap in bets with 90-day horizons for model-dependent features, longer for workflow and data investments
Capability insurance: design features so a better model improves them automatically (better retrieval, cleaner evals) rather than requiring rebuilds
Two-track roadmap: track one exploits today's models (ship now), track two prepares for next-gen capabilities (data pipelines, evals, UX patterns)
Kill criteria up front: define what 'the model got good enough to obsolete this' looks like, so you pivot deliberately instead of defensively

example.code:
Roadmap format:
  NOW (ship): prompt-based features on current models
  NEXT (build): eval harness, feedback loops, data pipelines
  LATER (bet): agent workflows when reliability crosses 95%
  KILL IF: frontier model ships native support for X

Every bet carries its kill condition.
example.walkthrough: The roadmap is a portfolio, not a promise: model-dependent bets are options, and options need expiry dates. Review quarterly against actual model releases — the labs' changelogs are your roadmap's weather report.

pitfalls: 12-month roadmaps assuming today's model capabilities
Building elaborate scaffolding around a weakness the next model release fixes
No kill criteria — zombie features nobody will retire
lessons.try_it: Write kill criteria for two model-dependent features on a roadmap you know.

lessons.title: Pricing the AI Value: Capturing What You Create
concepts: AI products create value in strange shapes: time saved, errors avoided, capacity unlocked — price the outcome the buyer feels, not the tokens you burn
The value conversation happens before the pricing page: discovery must surface the dollar cost of the pain, or every price feels expensive
Anchor on the alternative: the buyer's comparison is not your competitor — it is hiring, outsourcing, or living with the pain — price against THAT
Leave money on the table deliberately at first: early pricing buys learning and logos; you can raise prices on proven value, but you cannot un-churn sticker shock

example.code:
Value pricing worksheet:
  Pain: 500 tickets/mo x 12 min x $45/hr loaded = $4,500/mo
  AI resolves 60% -> $2,700/mo value
  Price at 20-30% of value: $540-810/mo
  Buyer ROI: 3-5x. Your margin: 80%.

Price the pain, not the tokens.
example.walkthrough: If you cannot articulate the buyer's ROI in one sentence, you are not ready to price — go back to discovery. Pricing without a value story is just a number waiting to be negotiated down.

pitfalls: Cost-plus pricing on tokens — races to the bottom as models get cheaper
Pricing before quantifying the buyer's pain
Optimizing early pricing for margin instead of learning
lessons.try_it: Write the one-sentence ROI story for an AI feature: whose pain, what dollar value, what price?

lessons.title: Discovering AI Jobs-to-Be-Done
concepts: Watch the work, not the wishlist: shadow users doing the task today and log where they hesitate, copy-paste, or ask a colleague — those are the automation seams
Ask about the last time, not the hypothetical: 'walk me through the last ticket you escalated' beats 'would you use an AI that...' — stated preference for AI is wildly inflated
Quantify the pain before building: frequency × duration × error cost. A daily 20-minute pain outranks a monthly 2-hour pain for AI products (habit formation needs repetition)
Segment by AI-readiness: some users want autopilot, others want a copilot, some want nothing automated — one product can serve all three with modes, but research must find the split

example.code:
Interview guide (30 min):
  1. Last time you did [task]? Walk me through it.
  2. Where did you get stuck or annoyed?
  3. What did you do about it? (workaround = real pain)
  4. If this took 10 seconds, what would you do with the time?

Workarounds reveal willingness to pay.
example.walkthrough: Recruit outside the AI-enthusiast bubble: your early volunteers overstate comfort with automation. The skeptical veteran who has seen three 'AI' tools fail is your most valuable interview — they describe the trust bar you must clear.

pitfalls: Asking 'would you use an AI for this?' — everyone says yes, nobody means it
Interviewing only enthusiasts — the trust bar looks lower than it is
Skipping quantification — unmeasured pain cannot prioritize a roadmap
lessons.try_it: Write 4 'last time' interview questions for one workflow you want to automate.

lessons.title: Wizard-of-Oz Testing for AI
concepts: Test the experience before the model: a human behind the curtain produces the 'AI' output, letting you validate desirability and UX in days instead of model-months
Fake the right layer: the wizard must produce realistic output quality — including realistic ERRORS — or you will validate a fantasy
Measure what matters: task completion, time saved, trust behaviors (did they verify? did they edit?), and the correction rate your pipeline must handle
Debrief honestly: reveal the wizard, then ask what would change if it were instant, dumber, or wrong 10% of the time — you are testing the concept's robustness, not the demo

example.code:
WOZ protocol:
  Day 1-2: script the wizard's responses + error rate (e.g., 85% good)
  Day 3-5: 8 users, real tasks, wizard in another room
  Metrics: completion, time, edits, trust checks
  Debrief: reveal + 'what if it were wrong 1 in 10?'

Kill or commit in one week.
example.walkthrough: The wizard's error rate is the most important parameter: testing with a perfect wizard validates a product you cannot build. Set the error rate to your realistic model target and watch whether users still get value — that is the real test.

pitfalls: Wizard too perfect — validating an unbuildable product
Never debriefing — users feel deceived when they find out later
Testing UI polish instead of the core value exchange
lessons.try_it: Design a 1-week Wizard-of-Oz test for one AI feature: wizard script, error rate, metrics, debrief questions.

lessons.title: Mental Models: What Users Believe the AI Is
concepts: Users arrive with a mental model — intern, oracle, search engine, colleague — and it dictates how they prompt, what they trust, and how they react to errors
Mismatched models cause the failure modes: the 'oracle' user never verifies; the 'intern' user over-verifies and gets no leverage; the 'search' user writes keywords instead of tasks
Shape the model deliberately: onboarding copy, example prompts, and the UI's language ('draft,' 'suggest,' 'suggestion') teach users what the system is
Test comprehension, not satisfaction: ask users to predict what the AI will do in a new situation — accurate predictions mean the mental model is right

example.code:
Model-shaping copy:
  Oracle framing: 'Ask anything, get answers' -> overtrust
  Copilot framing: 'Drafts for you to review' -> calibrated
  Tool framing: 'Summarize, extract, draft' -> task-shaped prompts

Every word teaches the model.
example.walkthrough: Revisit mental models after errors: a single confident hallucination can flip a user from 'copilot' to 'untrustworthy toy' permanently. The recovery UX — acknowledgment, correction, explanation — is where the model gets rebuilt.

pitfalls: Letting marketing write 'AI that knows everything' while the product needs verification
Measuring NPS instead of model accuracy — satisfaction hides misunderstanding
One mental model for all users — novices and experts need different framing
lessons.try_it: Write three onboarding sentences that teach the 'draft for review' mental model for an AI feature.

lessons.title: Measuring AI Product-Market Fit
concepts: The AI PMF question is not 'do they like it' but 'does it change behavior': retention of activated users, frequency of the core AI action, and corrections trending down
Sean Ellis test, AI edition: 'how disappointed if this AI feature disappeared?' — 40%+ 'very disappointed' still applies, but segment by heavy vs light users
Leading indicators: correction/edit rates falling, prompt sophistication rising, sharing of outputs, expansion to new use cases unprompted
Cohort the truth: AI products often show great week-1 novelty then decay — measure 8-week retained behavior, not launch-week excitement

example.code:
AI PMF scorecard:
  8-wk retention of activated: ___% (target 40%+)
  Core AI actions / user / week: ___ (rising?)
  Correction rate trend: ___ (falling?)
  'Very disappointed': ___% (target 40%+)
  Unprompted expansion: ___ cases

Behavior over attitudes.
example.walkthrough: Beware the novelty curve: AI demos produce a dopamine spike that looks like PMF for 2-3 weeks. Make every PMF claim from cohorts past week 8, and distrust any metric that peaks at launch.

pitfalls: Declaring PMF from launch-week engagement
Tracking logins instead of the core AI action
Averaging heavy and light users — the segments tell different stories
lessons.try_it: Draft the AI PMF scorecard for a product you know: fill what you can, mark what you would instrument.

lessons.title: Researching Trust Over Time
concepts: Trust in AI is longitudinal: first impressions form in minutes, but durable trust builds (or erodes) over weeks of observed behavior — one-shot studies miss the curve
Diary studies reveal the trust trajectory: ask users to log AI interactions for 2-4 weeks — you will see the honeymoon, the first betrayal, and the new equilibrium
The betrayal moment is the richest data: when the AI fails a user, what do they do — abandon, work around, or forgive? The recovery design decides which
Re-research after errors ship: every major AI failure is a natural experiment — interview affected users within days, while the memory is fresh

example.code:
Longitudinal protocol:
  Week 1: baseline mental model interview
  Weeks 2-3: diary (log each AI use: task, result, trust 1-5)
  Week 4: betrayal interview ('tell me about a time it failed')
  Analysis: plot trust over time; find the inflection points

Trust is a time series, not a snapshot.
example.walkthrough: Do not only study your successes: recruit users who churned or reduced usage — the ex-user interview is where the trust failures live. Current users have survivorship bias baked in.

pitfalls: One-shot usability tests as the only trust research
Studying only happy, retained users
Never re-interviewing after a shipped failure
lessons.try_it: Design a 4-week diary study for one AI feature: what gets logged, and what inflection points do you expect?

lessons.title: Positioning: Say What It Does, Not What It Is
concepts: Position on the outcome, not the technology: 'cut support handle time 40%' beats 'GPT-powered semantic copilot' — buyers buy results, not architectures
Name the enemy: the clearest positioning contrasts with the status quo ('replace the 6-tool swivel chair') rather than listing features
AI-washing destroys trust: if the AI is a thin wrapper, say what it actually does — oversold AI that underdelivers poisons the whole category for you
One persona, one pain, one promise: the homepage speaks to a single buyer with a single urgent problem before it speaks to everyone

example.code:
Positioning statement:
  For [support leaders drowning in ticket backlog]
  who [need faster resolution without hiring],
  [Acme Copilot] is [the AI agent]
  that [resolves 60% of tickets autonomously],
  unlike [chatbot widgets that deflect nothing].
example.walkthrough: Test positioning with the 'so what' drill: read every homepage claim and ask 'so what?' until you reach a business outcome. If you cannot get there in two steps, the claim is technology in a trench coat.

pitfalls: Leading with the model name instead of the outcome
Claiming 'AI-powered' for a rules engine with a classifier
Positioning to everyone — which positions to no one
lessons.try_it: Write a positioning statement for an AI product you know using the template above.

lessons.title: Launch Strategy: Sequenced, Not Big Bang
concepts: Lighthouse customers first: 3-5 design partners who feel the pain acutely, get white-glove onboarding, and become case studies — their logos open every later door
Waitlist as instrument: a waitlist is not hype, it is a prioritized interview pipeline — segment by persona and pain, onboard in cohorts, learn between each
Launch in waves: private alpha (friendly users, broken things OK) → public beta (positioned, instrumented) → GA (SLA, support, packaging) — each wave has exit criteria
The launch artifact that matters most is proof: one quantified customer story beats ten feature announcements

example.code:
Wave plan:
  Alpha (4 wks): 5 design partners, weekly calls, no SLA
  Beta (8 wks): 100 users from waitlist, usage instrumentation
  GA: packaging + pricing live, support staffed, 2 case studies

Exit criteria written before each wave.
example.walkthrough: Resist launching to everyone at once: a big-bang launch spends your one moment of attention on a product that has not yet learned from real users. Sequenced waves convert attention into learning, then learning into proof, then proof into scale.

pitfalls: Big-bang launch with no design partners or proof
Waitlist as a vanity metric with no segmentation or learning loop
Skipping exit criteria — waves blur into permanent beta
lessons.try_it: Draft exit criteria for moving an AI feature from private alpha to public beta.

lessons.title: Distribution: Where AI Products Actually Sell
concepts: Product-led growth: the product IS the sales motion — free tier, viral artifacts (shared reports, public dashboards), and upgrade prompts at value moments
Sales-led for enterprise: AI products with compliance needs sell through champions and security reviews — arm the champion with ROI docs and a security packet
Marketplace and ecosystem: list where buyers already shop (cloud marketplaces, app stores) — procurement is faster when the vendor is pre-approved
Partnerships: agencies, consultants, and platform partners sell your product inside their services — the highest-leverage channel once you have proof

example.code:
Channel fit:
  Prosumer/dev tool -> PLG + community
  Mid-market SaaS -> PLG + inside sales assist
  Enterprise AI -> sales-led + marketplace + partners

Match motion to buyer, not to fashion.
example.walkthrough: Pick channels by where your buyer's trust already lives: developers trust docs and peers, executives trust peers and analysts, IT trusts procurement vehicles. One channel done well beats three done thinly — sequence them as proof accumulates.

pitfalls: PLG motion for a product that requires a security review to adopt
Ignoring cloud marketplaces where your buyer already has committed spend
Partner program before you have a repeatable sale to hand partners
lessons.try_it: For one AI product, rank PLG, sales-led, marketplace, and partnerships by fit. Justify the top pick.

lessons.title: GTM Metrics: Activation to Expansion
concepts: Activation: the percentage of signups reaching the magic moment (first successful AI output) within the first session — the single most predictive GTM metric
Time-to-value: median minutes from signup to first meaningful result — every minute of setup friction compounds into churn
Net revenue retention (NRR): revenue from a cohort a year later including expansion minus churn — 120%+ means the product sells itself deeper
CAC payback: months of gross margin to repay acquisition cost — AI products with usage-based pricing must watch this as power users concentrate cost

example.code:
GTM dashboard:
  Activation (magic moment in session 1): 32% -> target 50%
  Time-to-value: 47 min -> target <15
  NRR: 118%
  CAC payback: 11 mo

Fix activation first — it multiplies everything downstream.
example.walkthrough: When GTM stalls, debug the funnel in order: acquisition → activation → retention → expansion. Most AI products do not have a traffic problem; they have an activation problem wearing a traffic costume. Fix the magic moment before buying more top of funnel.

pitfalls: Optimizing acquisition while activation sits at 15%
Celebrating logo count while NRR bleeds below 100%
No instrumentation on the magic moment itself
lessons.try_it: Define the magic moment and activation metric for an AI product you know.

lessons.title: Category Creation vs Capture
concepts: Category creators educate the market: expensive, slow, but the winner defines the buying criteria — only attempt with venture-scale funding and a genuinely new job-to-be-done
Category capturers ride existing demand: position against the known category ('the AI-native Zendesk') and win on the wedge — faster, cheaper, and legible to buyers
Most AI startups should capture, not create: buyers already budget for support software, analytics, and security — be the AI-native version, not a new line item
The naming decision is strategic: a new category name confuses procurement ('what budget does this come from?'); a known category name accelerates it

example.code:
Decision test:
  Do buyers already budget for this job? YES -> capture
  Is the job genuinely new (no budget exists)? -> create (with funding)
  Can you describe it in 5 words using known terms? YES -> capture

Clarity beats novelty in GTM.
example.walkthrough: If you choose creation, budget 18-24 months of education: analyst briefings, category content, and lighthouse proof. Creation without the education budget is just confusing marketing.

pitfalls: Inventing category names for a better version of existing software
No budget line for the purchase — deals stall in 'innovation' limbo
Creation ambition without education funding
lessons.try_it: Classify three AI products you know: category creators or capturers? Was the choice right?

lessons.title: Capstone: AI Product Launch — Overview
concepts: Your capstone: a launched AI product slice: framed problem, evaluated prototype, priced packaging, and a sequenced go-to-market plan
Break the build into phases: plan, build, secure, validate, document. Each phase maps to domains in this bootcamp
Document as you go — your write-up is the interview artifact that proves senior-level ownership
Done beats perfect: a working system with honest limitations beats an unfinished ambitious one

example.code:
Phase 1: Frame the problem: customer, job-to-be-done, pain quantification, and the AI 10x test
Phase 2: Build the evaluated slice: working prototype with golden-set evals and a measured baseline
Phase 3: Design the UX: trust-calibrated interface with provenance, gates, and feedback capture
Phase 4: Price it: unit economics model, tier packaging, and the free-to-paid path
Phase 5: Plan the launch: lighthouse sequence, proof assets, and GTM metrics dashboard
example.walkthrough: Treat each phase as a mini-project with a definition of done. Demo each phase working before moving on — integration surprises compound.

pitfalls: Starting to build before writing the plan — an hour of planning saves ten of rework
Skipping documentation until the end — you will forget why decisions were made
Gold-plating phase one while phase four remains untouched
lessons.try_it: Write the one-paragraph project plan: what you will build, in what phases, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Capstone: Validation and Demo
concepts: Validate every requirement with a test you can show: screenshots, command output, or a live demo
Prepare the 5-minute demo narrative: problem, approach, build, validation, lessons learned
Anticipate questions: know the trade-offs you made and what you would do with more time
Publish the write-up: architecture diagram, build log, validation evidence, reflection

example.code:
Demo script template:
  1. The problem (30s)
  2. Architecture overview (60s)
  3. Live walkthrough (2 min)
  4. Validation evidence (60s)
  5. What I would do next (30s)
example.walkthrough: A demo that only shows the happy path invites the hardest questions. Show one failure mode and how the system handles it — that is what interviewers remember.

pitfalls: Demoing without rehearsing — run it three times end-to-end first
Hiding limitations — name them before you are asked
No architecture diagram — draw the system before you demo it
lessons.try_it: Draft your 5-minute demo script for the capstone project.

lessons.title: Designing for Probabilistic Outputs
concepts: AI outputs are probabilistic, not deterministic: the same input can produce different answers, so the UI must never present AI output as verified fact
Show the seam: citations, source links, and confidence signals let users judge the output instead of blindly trusting it
Make correction cheap: an edit-and-retry affordance next to every generated artifact turns errors into training signal and keeps users in flow
Progressive disclosure: lead with the answer, reveal reasoning and sources on demand — experts want the chain, novices want the conclusion

example.code:
Chat UI response block:
  [Answer text]
  v Sources (3) | Confidence: High
  [Copy] [Regenerate] [Edit prompt] [Report issue]

Every generation carries its own correction tools.
example.walkthrough: Never render AI output with the visual authority of verified data — plain text without sources reads as truth. Pair every generation with provenance: where it came from, how confident the system is, and one click to challenge it.

pitfalls: Presenting generated text as fact with no sources or confidence signal
Burying the regenerate/correct controls three menus deep
Showing the full chain-of-thought — it leaks prompt internals and overwhelms
lessons.try_it: Sketch a response card for an AI summary feature: answer, sources, confidence, and correction controls.

lessons.title: Trust Calibration: Not Too Much, Not Too Little
concepts: Overtrust: users accept wrong outputs uncritically — caused by confident tone, clean formatting, and no visible uncertainty
Undertrust: users ignore or double-check everything — caused by one memorable failure or opaque behavior; kills adoption
Calibrated trust is the goal: users trust the system exactly as much as it deserves, varying by task risk and observed accuracy
Design levers: show uncertainty honestly, require confirmation for high-stakes actions, and surface track record ('94% of summaries accepted unchanged')

example.code:
Trust calibration matrix:
  High stakes + low confidence -> require human approval
  High stakes + high confidence -> show evidence, one-click confirm
  Low stakes + any confidence -> act, allow undo

Match friction to risk x uncertainty.
example.walkthrough: A polished confident tone is the fastest path to overtrust. Deliberately vary the presentation: tentative language and visible sourcing when uncertain, crisp delivery when the evidence is strong. The UI should feel like a smart colleague, not an oracle.

pitfalls: Confident tone on low-confidence outputs — the hallucination trap
Forcing manual review on everything — friction without risk justification
No track record shown — users cannot calibrate without observed accuracy
lessons.try_it: List three moments in your product where trust must be high, and design the friction each deserves.

lessons.title: Human-in-the-Loop Patterns
concepts: Human-in-the-loop (HITL): a person approves, edits, or rejects AI output before it takes effect — mandatory where errors are costly or irreversible
Gate tiers: auto-approve (low risk, reversible), one-click confirm (medium), dual approval (high stakes), hard block (never automate)
Review queues: batch low-urgency items for human review with triage (highest risk first), SLAs, and reviewer tooling that shows evidence inline
Escalation paths: the AI must know when it is out of its depth — low confidence, novel input, or conflicting sources should route to a human with full context

example.code:
Support copilot flow:
  Draft response -> confidence 0.92 -> agent one-click send
  Draft response -> confidence 0.61 -> agent must edit first
  Refund action -> always requires approval (irreversible)

Policy, not vibes, decides the gates.
example.walkthrough: Design the loop around the human's attention budget: every approval you demand spends trust. Reserve gates for decisions where a wrong AI call costs more than the reviewer's time — and instrument override rates to find gates that are pure theater.

pitfalls: Approving everything by default — the human becomes a rubber stamp in weeks
No escalation path — the AI guesses silently when confused
Review queues without triage — reviewers burn out on low-risk items
lessons.try_it: Draw the gate tiers for one AI feature: which actions auto-run, which need approval, which are blocked?

lessons.title: Feedback Loops: Turning Corrections into Quality
concepts: Every user correction is labeled data: thumbs up/down, edits, regenerations, and abandonments are the cheapest training signal you will ever get
Capture the delta, not just the vote: 'user edited the summary' is useful; the before/after diff is what improves the model
Close the loop visibly: 'Thanks — your correction improved summaries for everyone' turns a chore into a contribution and increases future feedback
Aggregate before acting: one user's complaint is noise; a cluster of similar corrections is a product defect with a fix

example.code:
Feedback taxonomy:
  Explicit: ratings, bug reports, preference picks
  Implicit: edits, regenerations, copy-paste, dwell, abandon
  Structured: side-by-side A/B choices on candidate outputs

Log all three; weight implicit highest at scale.
example.walkthrough: Instrument feedback from day one, even before you can act on it — retroactive instrumentation is impossible. But never train on raw user text without consent and PII scrubbing; the feedback pipeline is also a privacy surface.

pitfalls: Only a thumbs-down with no way to say what was wrong
Training on user corrections without consent or PII handling
Ignoring implicit signals — edits and regenerations outnumber votes 100:1
lessons.try_it: Design the feedback capture for one feature: what explicit, implicit, and structured signals will you log?

lessons.title: Error States: When the AI Fails Gracefully
concepts: AI fails differently than software: wrong answers look right, empty results look broken, and uncertainty looks like incompetence — each needs its own error pattern
The honest failure: 'I could not find a reliable answer in your documents' with next steps beats a hallucinated answer every time — design the no-answer state first
Partial failure patterns: show what succeeded, name what did not, and offer the recovery path ('3 of 5 sources searched — retry, narrow the question, or ask an expert')
Never dead-end: every AI error state offers an action — retry with guidance, rephrase help, escalate to a human, or continue manually with what exists

example.code:
Error pattern library:
  No sources: 'No relevant documents found. Try: [broader terms] [check spelling] [ask your admin to add docs]'
  Low confidence: answer shown WITH uncertainty + 'verify before using'
  Tool failure: 'Search is temporarily down — I can still draft from context. [Retry search]'

Failure is a designed state.
example.walkthrough: Test error states with real users before launch: the no-answer and low-confidence paths get 10x less design attention and 10x more user impact than the happy path. A graceful failure builds more trust than a lucky success.

pitfalls: Hallucinating instead of admitting no answer — the cardinal sin
Generic 'something went wrong' with no recovery action
Error states designed never, discovered in production
lessons.try_it: Design the no-answer state for a RAG feature: message, next steps, and escalation path.

lessons.title: Unit Economics: The Cost Behind Every Query
concepts: Every AI interaction has a marginal cost: input/output tokens, retrieval compute, reranking, and tool calls — know your fully-loaded cost per query before pricing anything
Gross margin math: (price per query − cost per query) / price per query. Healthy SaaS targets 75%+; AI products often start at 40-60% and engineer their way up
Cost levers: smaller models for easy tasks (routing), caching repeated queries, shorter context windows, and batching — each can cut cost 50-90% on eligible traffic
Power-law usage: the top 5% of users often drive 50%+ of inference cost — flat pricing subsidizes them with everyone else's margin

example.code:
Margin worksheet:
  Cost/query: $0.023 (tokens) + $0.004 (retrieval) = $0.027
  Price/query: $0.10 (usage tier)
  Gross margin: 73%
  At 10x volume with caching: cost -> $0.011, margin -> 89%
example.walkthrough: Model your unit economics on p95 usage, not averages — the heavy users define your margin. Revisit the model every time you change models, prompts, or retrieval depth; a 'small' prompt change can double token cost silently.

pitfalls: Pricing from averages while power users destroy margin
Forgetting retrieval/embedding/tool costs — tokens are only part of it
Never re-measuring after prompt changes
lessons.try_it: Estimate the fully-loaded cost per query for one AI feature you know: tokens in/out, retrieval, tools.

lessons.title: Pricing Models: Seat, Usage, Outcome
concepts: Per-seat: simple, predictable, familiar — but misaligned when AI does the work of ten seats; customers feel punished for efficiency gains
Usage-based (tokens, queries, tasks): aligns price with value and cost — but bills spike unpredictably, and finance teams hate surprises
Outcome-based (per resolution, per hire, per booked meeting): closest to value — but requires agreed measurement and puts delivery risk on you
Hybrid wins most AI deals: platform fee (predictability) + usage tiers (alignment) + overage (upside) — each part answers a different buyer objection

example.code:
Hybrid example:
  $499/mo platform (up to 5 seats, support, SLA)
  + $0.08 per resolved ticket
  + volume tiers: 10k+ tickets at $0.06
  Annual commit -> 15% discount

Predictable base, aligned variable.
example.walkthrough: Match the model to who signs: end users love seats, CFOs love predictable commits, operators love usage tied to their KPI. In enterprise deals, expect the buyer to ask for all three — design packaging so the answer is yes with one order form.

pitfalls: Pure per-seat for an automation product — you get paid less as you deliver more value
Pure usage with no cap or commit — finance kills the deal
Outcome pricing without a measurement both sides trust
lessons.try_it: Pick one AI feature and sketch seat, usage, and hybrid pricing for it. Which would the buyer choose?

lessons.title: Packaging: Good, Better, Best for AI
concepts: Gate on value metrics, not arbitrary limits: queries per month, data sources connected, automation actions — things that grow as the customer gets value
The AI-native wedge belongs in the middle tier: make 'Better' the obvious choice by putting the headline AI capability there, with 'Good' as the on-ramp
Add-ons monetize depth: extra data connectors, SSO/audit (enterprise), higher rate limits, dedicated models — each priced to the segment that needs it
Grandfather carefully: early users on generous terms are marketing; changing their deal is churn fuel — version your packaging instead

example.code:
Tier sketch:
  Starter $29: 500 queries/mo, 1 data source, community support
  Pro $99: 5k queries, 10 sources, API access, priority queue  <- wedge
  Enterprise: SSO, audit, VPC, custom retention, SLA

AI features concentrate upward with value.
example.walkthrough: Every tier boundary should answer 'who is this for?' in one sentence. If you cannot name the buyer for a tier, it is not a tier — it is a price list. Review packaging quarterly against actual usage: the most common upgrade trigger tells you where the real value gate is.

pitfalls: Gating on seats when value scales with usage
Putting the hero AI feature in the top tier only — nobody discovers it
Changing early adopters' pricing without versioning
lessons.try_it: Write the one-sentence 'who is this for' for three tiers of a hypothetical AI product.

lessons.title: From Free to Paid: The Conversion Engine
concepts: Free tiers are acquisition: cap them on the value metric (queries, not seats) so growth in usage naturally pushes toward paid
The value metric must be legible: users should feel the limit approaching as success ('we hit 1,000 summaries — time to upgrade'), not as punishment
Time-boxed trials beat freemium for complex AI: 14 days of full power creates the habit; freemium's thin slice may never show the magic
Expansion revenue is the real game: land with one team, expand on seats, usage, and new AI modules — net revenue retention above 120% is the benchmark

example.code:
Conversion levers:
  Usage emails at 70% and 95% of free quota
  In-product upgrade nudge at the moment of value ('this report used Pro features')
  Annual prepay discount at the upgrade moment
  Sales assist for accounts crossing 3x free limits
example.walkthrough: Instrument the free-to-paid funnel like a product surface: activation rate, time-to-first-value, quota-hit conversion. The single highest-leverage number is usually time-to-first-magic-moment — shorten it relentlessly.

pitfalls: Free tier so generous nobody ever upgrades
Upgrade prompts at moments of frustration instead of moments of value
No expansion path — every account is a one-time sale
lessons.try_it: Define the value metric and free-tier cap for an AI product you know. Where does the upgrade trigger fire?

lessons.title: Negotiating AI Deals: Procurement Realities
concepts: Enterprise AI deals die in procurement, not in pilots: security reviews, DPAs, data-processing terms, and model-training opt-outs — prepare the packet before the pilot ends
The training-data clause is the new battleground: buyers increasingly demand their data never train models — have the contractual language and the technical enforcement ready
Price the diligence: a 60-hour security review on a $10k deal is a loss — set minimums, use standardized packets, and qualify deal size against diligence cost early
Multi-year commits unlock everything: offer meaningful discounts for annual prepay — it funds the diligence, smooths revenue, and raises switching costs

example.code:
Deal readiness checklist:
  [ ] Security packet (SOC 2, pen test, architecture)
  [ ] DPA + training-data opt-out language
  [ ] Subprocessor list current
  [ ] ROI one-pager for the economic buyer
  [ ] Annual vs monthly pricing with commit tiers

Procurement is a product surface.
example.walkthrough: Start the security review in week one of the pilot, not week one of procurement: parallel tracks compress the 3-month stall into background noise. The champion who loves the product is your guide through their own buying process — equip them.

pitfalls: Discovering the security review after the verbal yes
Custom DPA negotiations on every small deal
No training-data clause — losing regulated buyers silently
lessons.try_it: Draft the training-data opt-out clause you would offer an enterprise buyer in one paragraph.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Model for the Job
concepts: No single model wins everywhere: frontier models lead on reasoning, small models win on latency, cost, and throughput — the choice is a tradeoff, not a ranking
Decide with evals, not vibes: run your golden set against 2-3 candidate models and compare quality-per-dollar on YOUR tasks, not public benchmarks
Latency budgets kill options fast: a 60-second report can use the smartest model; a chat response with a 2-second SLA probably cannot
Plan for model churn: abstract the model behind an interface so swapping providers or versions is a config change, not a rewrite

example.code:
Selection scorecard:
  Quality on golden set: A 94% / B 91% / C 82%
  Cost per 1k queries: A $4.20 / B $0.90 / C $0.12
  p95 latency: A 8.2s / B 2.1s / C 0.6s

Chat -> B. Batch reports -> A. Autocomplete -> C.
example.walkthrough: Benchmarks measure the model's test-taking; your evals measure your product. A model that tops public leaderboards can still fail your specific task — and a 'weaker' model fine-tuned on your domain can win where it counts.

pitfalls: Defaulting to the biggest model for every task — margin death by tokens
Choosing on benchmarks instead of your own evals
Hardcoding the model name through the codebase — migration becomes surgery
lessons.try_it: Build a 3-model scorecard for one feature you know: quality, cost, latency. Which wins?

lessons.title: API Reliability: Retries, Timeouts, Fallbacks
concepts: LLM APIs fail like any distributed dependency: rate limits, timeouts, 500s, and degraded latency — production code treats them as unreliable by default
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter on 429s and 5xx; never retry on 400s (your request is wrong) — and cap total retry budget so one bad call cannot cascade
Timeouts must be explicit: set per-request deadlines and fail fast to a fallback (cached response, simpler model, graceful degradation message)
Fallback chains: primary model → smaller/faster model → cached/stale response → honest 'unavailable' — each tier defined, tested, and monitored

example.walkthrough: Your fallback is only real if you have seen it work: inject failures in staging (kill the primary, throttle the API) and watch the chain engage. Untested fallbacks are comments, not reliability.

pitfalls: Infinite retries on rate limits — you become your own DDoS
No timeouts — one slow call hangs the whole request
Fallbacks that were never exercised — hope is not a strategy
lessons.try_it: Draw the fallback chain for one AI feature: what happens when the primary model is down?

lessons.title: Streaming, Function Calling, and Structured Output
concepts: Streaming (server-sent events): tokens arrive as generated — cuts perceived latency dramatically and lets users read while the model writes
Function/tool calling: the model emits structured calls (name + arguments) instead of prose — the bridge from language to action; validate every argument server-side
Structured output (JSON mode / schemas): constrain the response to a schema for reliable parsing — essential when downstream code consumes the output
Combine them: stream the user-facing text while function calls execute in parallel — the UI feels instant even when tools take seconds

example.code:
Parallel pattern:
  stream_text() -> user sees words immediately
  call_functions() -> [search_docs, calc] run concurrently
  render: text streams in; tool results slot into cards

Perceived latency ~= time to first token.
example.walkthrough: Never trust tool-call arguments blindly: the model can hallucinate parameter values with perfect JSON syntax. Schema validation is necessary but not sufficient — re-derive or verify critical arguments against your own data.

pitfalls: Waiting for the full response before rendering — users stare at spinners
Executing tool calls without validating arguments
Parsing free-text output with regex instead of using structured output
lessons.try_it: Sketch a UI that streams text while two tool calls run in parallel. What renders first?

lessons.title: System Prompts: Setting the Contract
concepts: The system prompt is the product spec the model actually reads: role, task, constraints, tone, and hard rules — everything the model must obey across all user inputs
Write rules as testable assertions: 'cite sources for every claim' beats 'be helpful' — vague instructions produce vague compliance
Order matters: put the most important constraints first AND last (primacy/recency), and repeat critical rules in different words
Version system prompts like code: git-tracked, reviewed, and tied to eval scores — a 'small wording tweak' can move quality 10 points

example.code:
System prompt skeleton:
  ROLE: You are a support copilot for Acme.
  TASK: Draft replies from the knowledge base.
  RULES: 1) Only use retrieved docs. 2) Cite doc IDs.
    3) If unsure, say so and escalate.
  TONE: concise, professional. FORMAT: ...
example.walkthrough: The system prompt is also an attack surface: users will try to override it ('ignore previous instructions'). Treat user input as data, never as instructions — and restate critical constraints where the model makes its final decision.

pitfalls: One giant paragraph of wishes instead of structured rules
Untestable instructions ('be smart', 'do your best')
Untracked prompt edits — nobody knows what changed when quality moved
lessons.try_it: Rewrite a vague system instruction ('be helpful and accurate') as 4 testable rules.

lessons.title: Few-Shot Examples That Actually Help
concepts: Few-shot examples teach by showing: 2-5 input/output pairs demonstrating the exact format, edge handling, and tone you want — more effective than paragraphs of description
Choose examples for coverage, not perfection: include one edge case and one 'what to do when unsure' example — the model generalizes from the boundaries
Keep examples diverse and short: near-duplicate examples waste tokens teaching the same thing twice; trim each to the minimal illuminating form
Examples go stale: when the task changes, the examples must change — stale few-shots actively teach the OLD behavior

example.walkthrough: Watch the token bill: few-shot examples ride along on EVERY request. Measure their marginal quality gain against their perpetual cost — sometimes one great example beats five good ones, and a fine-tune beats examples at scale.

pitfalls: Ten near-identical examples — token bloat with no new information
Only happy-path examples — the model never learns the edges
Stale examples contradicting the current instructions
lessons.try_it: Write 3 few-shot pairs for a classification task, including one edge case.

lessons.title: Chain-of-Thought and Reasoning Control
concepts: Chain-of-thought (CoT): asking the model to reason step-by-step before answering — dramatically improves accuracy on math, logic, and multi-step tasks
Reasoning effort is a dial: more reasoning tokens = better answers + higher cost and latency — tune it per task, not globally
Separate reasoning from the answer: have the model reason in a scratchpad, then produce a clean final response — users get clarity, you keep the audit trail
Do not expose raw CoT to users by default: it leaks prompt internals, confuses non-experts, and can contain unfiltered intermediate claims

example.code:
Pattern:
  Step 1 (hidden): 'Reason step by step in <scratchpad>.'
  Step 2 (shown): 'Based on the reasoning, give the final answer
    with citations.'

Accuracy from the scratchpad; trust from the clean answer.
example.walkthrough: CoT is not a truth serum: models can produce confident reasoning for wrong conclusions. Verify the final answer against evidence (retrieval, tools, tests) — reasoning traces explain the answer, they do not guarantee it.

pitfalls: Zero reasoning on multi-step tasks — fast wrong answers
Max reasoning everywhere — latency and cost explode
Showing raw chain-of-thought to end users
lessons.try_it: Take a 3-step reasoning task and split it into hidden scratchpad + clean final answer.

lessons.title: Prompt Versioning and Regression Testing
concepts: Prompts are code: version them in git, review changes, and never edit production prompts without a test run — 'just a wording tweak' is a deployment
Every prompt change runs the golden set first: quality delta per prompt version is the metric; ship only on neutral-or-better
A/B prompts in production: route a slice of traffic to the candidate, compare real user signals (correction rates, satisfaction) — evals predict, production decides
Keep a prompt changelog: what changed, why, eval delta, who approved — when quality regresses at 2 AM, the changelog is the first suspect

example.code:
Prompt CI:
  1. Edit prompt on a branch
  2. CI runs golden set (200 cases) on old vs new
  3. Report: quality +2.1%, cost +4%, latency +0.3s
  4. Human reviews diff + delta -> merge

Prompts ship like software because they are.
example.walkthrough: Golden sets rot: as the product and users evolve, last quarter's goldens stop representing reality. Refresh a slice of the golden set monthly from real production traffic — with human-verified answers.

pitfalls: Editing production prompts directly with no test
No changelog — regressions are mysteries
Golden set from launch day, never refreshed
lessons.try_it: Design prompt CI for one feature: what runs on every prompt change?

lessons.title: Chunking Strategies
concepts: Chunking decides what the retriever can find: too large and the signal drowns in noise; too small and context shatters across fragments
Respect document structure: chunk by semantic units (sections, paragraphs, Q&A pairs) — never mid-sentence — and keep titles/headers attached to their chunks
Overlap windows (10-20%) preserve cross-boundary context; metadata (doc title, date, section path) on every chunk enables filtering and better citations
Tune chunk size to the task: 200-400 tokens for precise Q&A, larger for summarization — then measure retrieval hit rate, not aesthetics

example.code:
Chunk spec:
  splitter: by markdown header (h2), max 350 tokens
  overlap: 50 tokens
  metadata: {doc_id, title, section, updated_at}
  filter: exclude chunks < 40 tokens (boilerplate)

Measured: recall@5 = 0.91 on goldens.
example.walkthrough: The chunking that looks cleanest is rarely the chunking that retrieves best. Let the eval decide: ablate chunk sizes against your golden set and pick the winner — then re-tune when the corpus changes shape.

pitfalls: Fixed 1000-token chunks with no overlap — context shatters
Stripping headers/metadata — chunks lose their identity
Never measuring retrieval quality after choosing a strategy
lessons.try_it: Take one long document and chunk it two ways; which preserves answerable units better?

lessons.title: Embeddings and Vector Search
concepts: Embeddings turn text into vectors where meaning ≈ distance: the retriever finds chunks 'near' the query in semantic space, not keyword space
Choose the embedding model deliberately: domain-tuned or recent general models beat legacy defaults; test retrieval recall on YOUR corpus, not a benchmark
Top-k is a tradeoff: k=3 is precise but brittle, k=20 is comprehensive but noisy and token-expensive — start at 5-8 and tune against evals
Normalize and version embeddings: changing the embedding model requires re-indexing everything — track the model version with the index

example.code:
Retrieval pipeline:
  query -> embed (model v3) -> ANN search (k=6)
  -> similarity scores [0.91, 0.87, 0.83, 0.71, ...]
  -> threshold 0.75 -> 3 chunks to reranker

Scores are relative; calibrate the threshold on goldens.
example.walkthrough: Vector search fails gracefully and silently: it always returns SOMETHING, even when nothing is relevant. A similarity threshold plus a 'no relevant sources found' path is what separates RAG from confident hallucination with extra steps.

pitfalls: No similarity threshold — irrelevant chunks always injected
Embedding model upgraded without re-indexing — silent corruption
Judging embeddings by benchmark instead of your retrieval recall
lessons.try_it: Define the 'no relevant sources' UX for a RAG feature: what does the user see?

lessons.title: Hybrid Search: Dense + Sparse
concepts: Dense (vector) search understands meaning but fumbles exact terms — product codes, names, IDs; sparse (BM25/keyword) nails exact terms but misses paraphrase
Hybrid = both, fused: run vector and keyword retrieval in parallel, merge with reciprocal rank fusion — each covers the other's blind spot
When hybrid wins most: technical docs, SKUs, error codes, legal text — anywhere precise terminology coexists with natural-language questions
Tune the fusion weight: keyword-heavy corpora (parts catalogs) want more sparse weight; conceptual corpora (guides) want more dense — measure on goldens

example.code:
Hybrid flow:
  query: 'PR-4500 reset procedure'
  dense top-6: [manual sec 4.2, ...] (misses the code)
  sparse top-6: [PR-4500 spec sheet, ...] (nails the code)
  fused: spec sheet #1, manual #2 -> answer cites both
example.walkthrough: Hybrid doubles your retrieval knobs — and your tuning surface. Start with 50/50 fusion, measure, then adjust; resist tuning weights by gut feel on five queries.

pitfalls: Pure vector search on a parts catalog — SKUs never match
Pure keyword on conceptual questions — paraphrases miss
Fusion weights set once, never measured
lessons.try_it: Name one query type in your domain where dense fails and one where sparse fails.

lessons.title: Reranking and Context Assembly
concepts: Reranking: a second, smarter pass over the top-N retrieved chunks — cross-encoder or LLM judge re-scores relevance; the single highest-ROI retrieval upgrade
Retrieve-then-rerank pattern: cheap ANN gets 30 candidates, expensive reranker picks the best 5 — quality of a big context window at a fraction of the token cost
Context assembly: order chunks by relevance, dedupe near-duplicates, attach citations (doc_id + span), and budget tokens — the prompt gets evidence, not a dump
Lost-in-the-middle: models attend to context edges more than the middle — put the most critical chunk first, and keep total context lean

example.code:
Assembly:
  1. ANN top-30 (cheap)
  2. Rerank -> top-5 (cross-encoder)
  3. Dedupe (similarity > 0.95)
  4. Order by score desc, cite [doc:span]
  5. Token budget: 4k max, truncate lowest first

Precision where it matters.
example.walkthrough: Reranking adds latency — measure it. If the reranker costs 800ms for +2% recall, it may lose to simply retrieving better chunks. Every stage in the pipeline must justify its milliseconds against the eval delta.

pitfalls: Dumping 20 raw chunks into the prompt — token bonfire
No dedupe — three near-identical chunks eat the budget
Reranker added without measuring latency cost
lessons.try_it: Design the context assembly for a RAG prompt: retrieval depth, rerank cutoff, token budget.

lessons.title: The ReAct Loop: Reason, Act, Observe
concepts: ReAct = the agent's heartbeat: reason about the goal, take an action (tool call), observe the result, repeat until done or stuck
The loop needs bounds: max iterations, max wall-clock time, and max cost — an unbounded loop is a billing incident waiting for a trigger
Observation quality decides everything: tool outputs must be concise, structured, and error-explicit — a 10k-token dump per step drowns the reasoning
Stuck detection: same action twice, no progress in N steps, or looping tool calls → break out, summarize, and escalate to the user with options

example.code:
Loop skeleton:
  for step in range(MAX_STEPS=12):
    thought = reason(goal, history)
    action = pick_tool(thought)
    obs = execute(action)  # structured, truncated
    history.append((thought, action, obs))
    if done(obs): break
  else: escalate(summary(history))
example.walkthrough: Log every loop iteration with timestamps and token counts: when an agent goes wrong in production, the trace is the only debugger you have. Loops without traces are mysteries; loops with traces are fixable.

pitfalls: No max iterations — runaway loops burning budget
Raw tool dumps as observations — context window flooded
No stuck detection — the agent retries the same failing call forever
lessons.try_it: Write the stuck-detection rules for an agent loop: which patterns trigger escalation?

lessons.title: Tool Design: Giving Agents Hands
concepts: Tools are the agent's API to the world: each tool needs a name, a precise description (when to use it), typed parameters, and clear error semantics
Fewer, composable tools beat many narrow ones: search_docs(query, filters) beats search_by_title, search_by_tag, search_by_author — the model picks better from a short list
Tools must be idempotent-aware: mark read vs write tools; writes need confirmation policies and dry-run modes — the agent WILL call them with surprising arguments
Error messages are instructions: 'order 123 not found' teaches nothing; 'order 123 not found — try list_orders(customer_id) or check the ID format' teaches the recovery

example.code:
Tool spec:
  name: lookup_order
  desc: 'Fetch order by ID. Use after extracting an order ID from the user.'
  params: {order_id: string (format ORD-\d+)}
  errors: NOT_FOUND -> suggest list_orders; INVALID_FORMAT -> show format
  side_effects: none (read-only)
example.walkthrough: Design tools for the model's failure modes: it will pass malformed arguments, call tools in the wrong order, and retry failures verbatim. Defensive tool design — validation, helpful errors, idempotency — is where agent reliability is actually built.

pitfalls: 30 overlapping tools — the model picks wrong constantly
Write tools with no confirmation or dry-run
Cryptic error messages — the agent cannot self-correct
lessons.try_it: Spec one tool for an agent you know: name, description, params, errors, side effects.

lessons.title: Planning vs Reacting: Agent Architectures
concepts: Reactive (ReAct): decide each step from current state — simple, robust, but myopic on long tasks and burns tokens re-reasoning
Plan-then-execute: decompose the goal into a plan first, then execute steps — better for multi-stage tasks, but brittle when the world changes mid-plan
Plan + replan: generate a plan, execute, and replan when observations diverge — the pragmatic middle for real-world tasks
Choose by task shape: single-tool lookups → reactive; 5+ dependent steps → plan-then-execute; dynamic environments → plan with replanning triggers

example.code:
Decision guide:
  'Summarize this doc' -> single LLM call (no agent!)
  'Find the bug causing X' -> ReAct loop
  'Migrate this module' -> plan-then-execute
  'Handle this incident' -> plan + replan

Simplest architecture that works.
example.walkthrough: The most common agent mistake is using an agent at all: if the task is a fixed sequence, write code. Agents earn their cost only where the path is genuinely uncertain — every unnecessary loop iteration is latency, money, and failure surface.

pitfalls: Agent loops for fixed pipelines — expensive, flaky scripts
Pure reactive on 10-step tasks — loses the plot by step 6
Rigid plans in dynamic environments — no replanning trigger
lessons.try_it: Classify three tasks you know: no-agent, reactive, or planned? Justify each.

lessons.title: Guardrails for Autonomous Agents
concepts: Least privilege per tool: the agent gets exactly the permissions its task needs — read-only where possible, scoped writes where not, nothing ambient
Action policies: which actions auto-run, which need approval, which are forbidden — enforced in code around the agent, not in the prompt
Blast-radius caps: per-run spending limits, rate limits on external actions, and kill switches — a compromised or confused agent must fail small
Audit everything: immutable log of thoughts, tool calls, arguments, and results — the record that makes incidents explainable and liability manageable

example.code:
Guardrail stack:
  1. Prompt: instructions (weakest, advisory)
  2. Tool gating: approval tiers in code
  3. Policy engine: allow/deny lists per action
  4. Sandbox: network + filesystem containment
  5. Audit log: immutable, timestamped

Defense in depth, not in prompt.
example.walkthrough: Prompts are not guardrails: 'do not delete files' in the system prompt is a suggestion the model may ignore under confusion or injection. Real guardrails live in code — the tool layer, the policy engine, the sandbox — where the model cannot negotiate with them.

pitfalls: 'Be careful' in the prompt as the only safety measure
Agent with production database write access and no approval tier
No audit log — incidents are unreconstructable
lessons.try_it: Design the guardrail stack for one agent: what is gated, capped, sandboxed, and logged?

lessons.title: Golden Datasets: Building the Ground Truth
concepts: Golden sets are the foundation of every eval: input → expected output pairs, human-verified, covering the task's real distribution — including the hard cases
Build from production: sample real user inputs, have experts write/verify the answers — synthetic-only goldens test the generator's imagination, not your users
Stratify by difficulty and type: factual lookup, reasoning, edge cases, adversarial — a golden set of 200 easy cases gives false confidence
Treat goldens as living: add every production failure as a new golden case — the set grows teeth with each incident

example.code:
Golden case format:
  {id, input, expected, sources: [doc spans],
   difficulty: hard, category: edge,
   added: 2026-10-03, reason: 'prod incident #482'}

Every failure becomes a permanent test.
example.walkthrough: Golden answers need the same rigor as production data: have a second expert verify a sample, track inter-rater agreement, and version the set. A golden set with wrong answers is worse than none — it trains you to optimize toward error.

pitfalls: 200 trivial cases — 100% pass, zero information
Synthetic-only inputs — real user distribution untested
Golden answers never verified — optimizing toward mistakes
lessons.try_it: Draft 5 golden cases for one AI feature, including one adversarial input.

lessons.title: LLM-as-Judge: Calibrating Automated Scoring
concepts: LLM judges scale evaluation: a strong model scores outputs on rubrics (accuracy, groundedness, tone) — thousands of cases overnight, no human bottleneck
Calibrate before trusting: have the judge score 100 human-graded cases first — measure agreement (Cohen's kappa); below ~0.7 the judge is decoration
Judges have biases: verbosity bias (longer = better), position bias (first option wins), self-preference — mitigate with rubrics, randomization, and blind scoring
Use judges for ranking, humans for truth: judges reliably order A > B; use humans to verify the absolute quality bar and to audit the judge quarterly

example.code:
Judge prompt:
  RUBRIC: groundedness 1-5 (every claim cited?)
  Score the RESPONSE against SOURCES.
  Penalize: uncited claims (-2), wrong citations (-3).
  Output: {score, reasoning, failed_checks[]}

Rubric + evidence, never vibes.
example.walkthrough: Never let the same model grade its own homework unmonitored: self-grading inflates scores. Use a different (ideally stronger) model as judge, blind the judge to the source, and spot-check with humans continuously.

pitfalls: Uncalibrated judge — scores that mean nothing
Same model judging itself — grade inflation
Free-form 'rate this 1-10' with no rubric — noise
lessons.try_it: Write a 3-criterion rubric for judging summaries in your domain.

lessons.title: Regression Testing for Prompts and Models
concepts: Every prompt edit, model swap, or retrieval change is a deployment: run the full golden set before and after, and ship only on neutral-or-better quality
Track the delta, not just the score: '+2% overall, −8% on edge cases' is a regression hiding in an average — stratify results by category
Pin model versions in production: auto-updating to the latest model is auto-deploying untested changes — upgrade deliberately with full evals
Canary the rollout: 5% of traffic on the new version, compare live signals (correction rates, latency, cost) — evals predict, production decides

example.code:
Regression report:
  Overall: 91.2% -> 92.0% (+0.8)
  Factual: +1.2 | Reasoning: +0.5 | Edge: -6.0 !!
  Cost/query: $0.031 -> $0.042 (+35%)
  VERDICT: BLOCKED — edge regression

Stratification caught what the average hid.
example.walkthrough: Evals must run in CI, not in notebooks: the moment evaluation is a manual chore, it stops happening. Automate the golden run on every prompt/model/retrieval change, and make the delta report a required check on the PR.

pitfalls: Shipping prompt tweaks without running evals
Overall-score-only reporting — category regressions hidden
Auto-upgrading model versions in production
lessons.try_it: Design the eval gate for prompt changes: what runs, what blocks, who approves?

lessons.title: Human Evaluation: When Only People Will Do
concepts: Humans are the ground truth for taste, tone, and trust: automated metrics cannot tell you if the response FEELS right to a customer
Design the task carefully: side-by-side blind comparisons with clear rubrics beat absolute ratings — 'which is better and why' produces signal, 'rate 1-5' produces noise
Sample strategically: humans grade the cases automation cannot — novel failures, high-stakes outputs, and a random slice to audit the automated judges
Respect rater time: clear guidelines, example judgments, and calibration rounds — noisy instructions produce noisy labels, and noisy labels poison everything downstream

example.code:
Human eval protocol:
  1. Blind A/B pairs (order randomized)
  2. Rubric: accuracy, tone, usefulness (forced choice + why)
  3. 3 raters per item; majority + agreement tracked
  4. Disagreements -> guideline refinement

Signal in, signal out.
example.walkthrough: Human eval is expensive — spend it where it compounds: on the golden answers themselves, on auditing the LLM judge, and on the failure modes that matter most. Grading 10,000 routine cases by hand is budget burned; grading the right 200 is infrastructure.

pitfalls: Absolute 1-5 ratings with no rubric — pure noise
Single rater per item — no agreement measurement
Humans grading what automation already measures well
lessons.try_it: Design a blind A/B human eval for one output type: rubric, sampling, rater count.

lessons.title: Spec-Driven Development with AI
concepts: Write the spec first, generate second: a precise spec (inputs, outputs, edge cases, constraints) turns the AI from a guesser into an implementer
Specs are the review surface: reviewing a 30-line spec catches design errors that reviewing 500 generated lines will miss — thinking scales better than reading
Iterate on the spec, not the code: when output is wrong, fix the specification's ambiguity first — regenerating from a vague spec just rolls the dice again
Acceptance criteria are executable: tests written from the spec BEFORE generation give you an objective verdict on the output

example.code:
Workflow:
  1. Write spec: function, inputs/outputs, 5 edge cases
  2. Write 3 acceptance tests from the spec
  3. Generate implementation
  4. Run tests -> fail? fix the SPEC, regenerate
  5. Review the diff like a colleague's PR

The spec is the source of truth.
example.walkthrough: The spec habit compounds: good specs become documentation, onboarding material, and regression protection. Teams that spec-first report the AI 'getting smarter' — it did not; the instructions got clearer.

pitfalls: Generating from a one-line prompt — lottery coding
Fixing generated code by hand instead of fixing the spec
No acceptance tests — 'looks right' as QA
lessons.try_it: Write a spec (with 5 edge cases) for a small function before generating it.

lessons.title: Reviewing AI-Generated Code Like a Senior
concepts: AI code needs senior review, not rubber stamps: it is syntactically fluent and semantically plausible — the most dangerous combination for bugs
Review checklist: correctness on edge cases, error handling, security (injection, auth, secrets), performance cliffs, and dependency choices — the model optimizes for plausible, not for right
Watch for confident nonsense: invented APIs, wrong-but-plausible library calls, and subtly-off algorithms — verify every external reference
The author is still you: generated code you merge is code you own — if you cannot explain it, do not ship it

example.code:
Review pass:
  1. Run it — does it work on the happy path?
  2. Edge cases from the spec — all covered?
  3. Errors: every failure mode handled or surfaced?
  4. Security: inputs validated? secrets safe?
  5. Deps: every import real and necessary?

Fluency is not correctness.
example.walkthrough: Set the team norm explicitly: AI-generated PRs get MORE scrutiny, not less — and 'the AI wrote it' is never an explanation in a review thread. The reviewer must be able to defend every line.

pitfalls: Approving because 'it looks right' — fluency bias
Skipping security review on generated code
'The AI wrote it' as a review explanation
lessons.try_it: Review a piece of AI-generated code with the 5-point checklist. What did you catch?

lessons.title: Test Generation and Coverage Gaps
concepts: AI writes tests fast — and tests the happy path thoroughly while missing the edges: generated suites systematically under-cover error handling, concurrency, and boundary conditions
Direct the coverage: ask for tests per edge case from the spec, mutation-style ('what input breaks this?'), and property-based tests for invariants
Tests need review too: a passing generated test can assert the WRONG behavior — verify assertions against the spec, not against the implementation
Coverage metrics lie politely: 90% line coverage with zero edge-case tests is a green dashboard on a fragile codebase

example.code:
Test prompt:
  'Generate tests for these 5 edge cases [list].
   For each: arrange/act/assert.
   Also generate 3 inputs you expect to BREAK
   the implementation.'

Ask for adversarial tests explicitly.
example.walkthrough: The highest-value test habit with AI: generate the tests FIRST from the spec, watch them fail, then generate the implementation. Failing-first tests turn the AI's optimism into a verifiable contract.

pitfalls: Accepting generated tests without checking assertions
Happy-path-only suites — green and fragile
No adversarial/breaking inputs requested
lessons.try_it: Ask an AI for 3 inputs that would break a function you wrote. Were you surprised?

lessons.title: AI in Legacy Codebases
concepts: Legacy code is where AI pays best: explain-this-function, trace-this-flow, and find-all-callers turn weeks of archaeology into days
Context is the constraint: feed the model the relevant slice (call graph, related files, tests) — a 2M-line repo does not fit, but the 5 files that matter do
Verify against reality: generated explanations of legacy code can be confidently wrong about undocumented behavior — cross-check with tests and runtime
Modernize in slices: AI-assisted strangler-fig refactors (one module at a time, tests as the safety net) beat big-bang rewrites

example.code:
Legacy workflow:
  1. 'Explain module X and its 3 key invariants'
  2. Verify against tests + runtime behavior
  3. Write characterization tests (lock current behavior)
  4. AI-assisted refactor of ONE module
  5. Tests green -> commit; repeat

Tests are the safety net.
example.walkthrough: Characterization tests first, always: before the AI touches legacy code, lock current behavior in tests. Without them, 'refactoring' is just editing — and you will discover what the code did by breaking it.

pitfalls: AI refactor with no characterization tests — behavior changes silently
Trusting generated explanations of undocumented code
Big-bang AI rewrites of legacy systems
lessons.try_it: Pick one legacy function: have AI explain it, then verify the explanation against tests.
