simulations.title: The hallucinating support bot
simulations.brief: The support bot invents refund policies that don't exist. Tickets are escalating.

steps.symptom: The bot cites a '30-day no-questions refund policy'; the real policy is 14 days with conditions.
evidence:
Bot: 'Per our 30-day no-questions-asked refund policy...'

Actual policy doc: 14-day refunds, unopened items only.
options: Ground the bot: retrieve the policy doc and require the model to cite it before answering policy questions
Tell the bot to 'be more careful'
Add 'do not hallucinate' to the system prompt and ship
steps.explain: Vague instructions don't fix fabrication. Retrieval-grounding ties answers to the real document; citation makes the grounding checkable.

steps.symptom: Grounding added. Verify it holds on edge cases.
evidence: Q: 'Can I return opened software after 20 days?' → Bot cites the policy doc line: '14-day, unopened items only.'
options: Confirm the bot cites the doc and refuses to invent beyond it
Confirm the bot handles more tickets
steps.explain: The success metric is citation fidelity, not speed or tone. Grounded answers are checkable answers.

steps.symptom: Grounded answers verified. Lock it in.
evidence: 50 policy questions: 50 cite the doc, 0 fabrications.
options: Ship with the eval as the regression gate: any future prompt change must re-pass it
steps.explain: The eval is the contract. Prompt changes without re-running it are how hallucinations return silently.

simulations.debrief: Hallucinations are fixed with grounding (retrieve the doc), citation (make it checkable), and evals (make it a gate). Vibes-based prompting is not a fix.

simulations.title: Prompt iteration loop
simulations.brief: Restore the order of a disciplined prompt iteration loop.

steps.context: Arrange the prompt iteration steps in execution order.
items: Write the failing test case first
Draft the prompt change
Run the eval suite
Review the failures
Ship only when the eval passes

simulations.debrief: Failing case → change → eval → review → ship. Prompt engineering without an eval is editing blind.

simulations.title: Automate or escalate?
simulations.brief: Decide what the agent handles alone and what goes to a human.

steps.text: The agent can resolve password resets with 99% success. Route?

choices.label: Automate fully: high success, low blast radius, reversible
choices.feedback: Right: automatable when success is high and mistakes are cheap and reversible.

choices.label: Always escalate to a human
choices.feedback: Escalating a 99%-success reversible task wastes the automation's value.

choices.label: Automate without logging
choices.feedback: Automation without audit logs is unmanageable when it eventually errs.

steps.text: The agent drafts account-closure responses (irreversible, regulated). Route?

choices.label: Draft for human review: the agent prepares, a human approves — irreversible actions need a human gate
choices.feedback: Right: irreversible and regulated actions get human approval, with the agent doing the prep work.

choices.label: Automate fully — it's just text
choices.feedback: 'Just text' that closes accounts is an irreversible regulated action. Humans approve.

choices.label: Block the agent from touching closures at all
choices.feedback: Blocking loses the draft value; the middle path is draft-plus-approval.

simulations.debrief: Automate what's reversible and high-confidence; human-gate what's irreversible or regulated. The blast radius decides, not the model's confidence.

simulations.title: The eval that passes vacuously
simulations.brief: The eval suite is green but the product still hallucinates. The eval config has 2 bugs in 10 lines.

steps.config:
model: gpt-draft
cases: 50
assert: contains_any(['refund', 'policy', 'days'])
threshold: 0.0
# run: nightly
# owner: ml-team

issues.description: The assertion passes if the answer merely mentions 'refund', 'policy', or 'days' — a hallucinated answer containing those words passes.
issues.fix: Assert citation of the policy doc and factual agreement with it, not keyword presence.

issues.description: threshold: 0.0 means the suite passes even with zero passing cases — green by definition.
issues.fix: Set a real threshold (e.g. 0.95) so failures actually fail the suite.

simulations.debrief: Evals must be able to fail: assert facts (not keywords) and set thresholds above zero. A suite that can't go red is decoration.

sections.heading: Agent Loops
items: Agent loops need explicit bounds — max iterations (a circuit breaker on runaway reasoning), per-step timeouts (a hung tool shouldn't hang the agent), and progress detection (same action three times = stuck).
Least privilege applies to agents — each tool is both attack surface (prompt-injected instructions reaching delete_db) and confusion surface (40 similar tools → wrong-tool calls).
Tool design — stop conditions are part of the design, not pessimism. Design tools like API endpoints: minimal, well-described, permissioned.
Human-in-the-loop gates belong at irreversibility — sending, deleting, purchasing, publishing — actions with external consequences get approval; reads, drafts, and analysis run autonomously.
Common trap — detect the stuck pattern (same action, same error) and escalate: try a different approach N times, then stop and report.
Common trap — give the minimal tool set for the task, with narrowly-scoped permissions.
Common trap — the agent should act on everything autonomously.
Common trap — require human confirmation for irreversible/high-stakes actions (send, delete, purchase, publish).

The ReAct loop is plan → act → observe → re-plan — each observation updates the plan. Blindly executing a stale plan (editing the wrong file because step 2 assumed step 1's result) is the signature agent failure mode. The plan is a working hypothesis, not a contract.

sections.heading: Evals
items: Golden datasets — a golden dataset — curated inputs with expected outputs, covering typical cases, edge cases, and known failures — turns 'seems good' into a score.

LLM-as-judge works when treated as a measurement instrument — a detailed rubric (what earns each score), the reference sources for groundedness checks, and human spot-checks measuring judge-human agreement.

Eval CI — model selection is a three-way tradeoff: quality (eval score), cost per request (at your volume, 10x is real money), and latency (3.2s changes the UX). 'Eval once at launch' misses drift; 'eval on complaint' is incident-driven development.

Regression — evals in CI on every prompt/model change make AI behavior regression-tested like code: the PR shows the score delta before merge. Re-run it on every prompt/model change: improvements and regressions become visible numbers.
